title: Revealing the administrative process of data sharing: LLM-assisted topic modelling of COVID-19 Immunity Task Force Databank operations
text:
Data Source and Preprocessing
[6] This study analyzes email correspondence generated during the operations of the Canadian COVID-19 Immunity Task Force (CITF) Databank, a pan-Canadian initiative that integrated individual-level health records from partnering studies conducted across Canada between 2020 and 2025. The analytical corpus comprises emails from the inbox of the central CITF Databank operations manager responsible for coordinating data sharing with all partnering studies. Emails span the period from February 2021 to September 2025.
[7] Emails were preprocessed using a multi-step pipeline to remove non-substantive content and protect participant privacy. Rule-based cleaning steps removed text automatically inserted by email providers, meeting-invite text, forwarded-message headers, and institutional email signatures. All messages were de-identified using Microsoft Presidio (Alrazihi, Biswas, and George 2025; Kotevski et al. 2022), an open-source framework for automated detection and anonymization of personally identifiable information, with personal names, email addresses, and URLs replaced with anonymized placeholders. Duplicate messages were removed within studies using normalized text hashing. Documents were filtered to retain only emails with non-missing sent dates and appropriate length, excluding near-empty or excessively long messages. The CITF Databank operated bilingually; bilingual messages were processed to retain English content where identifiable, and remaining French text was translated into English using OPUS-MT neural machine translation. This pipeline yielded a final analytical sample of 6,833 emails involving 491 unique senders across 100 studies (see Figure 1).

title: Revealing the administrative process of data sharing: LLM-assisted topic modelling of COVID-19 Immunity Task Force Databank operations
text:
Data Analysis
[8] We evaluated four topic modeling approaches to identify the method best suited to this corpus: K-Means clustering, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), BERTopic, and Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) (Murshed et al. 2023; Zubiaga 2024). Methods were compared at their peak coherence score (c_v) using standard English stopwords as a baseline. NMF outperformed all alternatives (c_v = 0.654), while K-Means produced an overly dominant cluster (50.8% of emails), LDA showed the lowest coherence (c_v = 0.517), and BERTopic assigned 32.3% of emails as outliers. Following additional domain-specific stopword curation and part-of-speech filtering, NMF performance improved across all values of k tested (k = 5 to 20). Although k = 5 achieved the highest coherence (c_v = 0.820), it produced only five broad topics with 35.6% of emails in the largest cluster. We selected k = 14 as the optimal balance between coherence (c_v = 0.768, NPMI = 0.170), granularity (lowest maximum cluster size at 10.7%), and topic diversity (0.914) (Rahimi et al. 2024).
[9] To facilitate interpretation of the 14 NMF topics, we used a locally deployed open-source large language model to generate topic labels, thematic groupings, and topic descriptions (Wanna et al. 2024; Janssens, Bogaert, and Van den Poel 2025; Tan and D’Souza 2025). Four open-source models were evaluated: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9b-it, each receiving the top 5 keywords and 5 representative emails for all 14 topics simultaneously. Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct produced the most descriptive and semantically complete labels and was selected for subsequent steps. Using zero-shot prompts, the model was queried to: (1) generate 2–5 word topic labels from keywords and representative emails; (2) group labels into thematic categories; and (3) generate 2–3 sentence topic descriptions from keywords and up to 15 representative emails. Tasks were run across multiple temperature settings (0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7) and random seeds to ensure stability. All outputs were reviewed and refined by the research team to ensure face validity and alignment with domain knowledge. Local deployment ensured that no email data left secure servers at any stage of analysis.
[10] Email-to-topic assignments were based on a 15% probability threshold applied to the normalized NMF weight matrix. This threshold was selected to capture substantive secondary topic assignments while filtering out most tertiary contributions, and was validated through research team review of representative emails. Under this scheme, 27.3% of emails were assigned to a single topic, 47.6% to two topics, and 25.1% to three or more topics (mean = 2.01 topics per email).
[11] Across all four analyses (lifecycle phases, sender roles, gender, and topic co-occurrence), we report per-study median values rather than corpus-wide pooled values, to prevent high-volume studies and high-volume individual senders from dominating the across-study summary. For each analysis, the unit of replication is the study and the unit of analysis is the (study, attribute) cell, where attribute is the phase, role, gender, or topic pair being examined. Cells with fewer than five emails were excluded so that medians were not driven by one or two messages. The cell value computed within each (study, attribute) varies by analysis and is defined in the corresponding paragraphs below.
[12] To trace topic distribution across the data sharing lifecycle, each email was mapped to one of six sequential phases: Funding Start, Data Introduction, Data Sharing Agreement (DSA) Execution, Data Upload, Data Cataloguing, and Data Publication. Phase assignments were based on milestone dates recorded for each study. Seven studies were excluded from phase analysis due to non-sequential milestone dates, leaving 6,110 emails from 93 studies. For sender analysis, each email sender was classified into one of five categories based on their institutional role: Databank Secretariat, Study Staff, Study Investigators, External Partners, and Harmonization Group. A small residual “Other” category was excluded, leaving 6,789 emails from 100 studies.
[13] To examine the distribution of coordination labour by gender, sender first names were coded using a probabilistic approach combining the nomquamgender library (Van Buskirk, Clauset, and Larremore 2023) with manual corrections for ambiguous and non-Western names, achieving coverage of 95.8% of emails (6,545 of 6,833). Gender was classified as women or men; non-binary and gender-diverse identities are not captured by this method, which represents a limitation of the approach.
[14] Relationships between topics were investigated by computing normalized pairwise co-occurrence scores across all 14 topics (Stevenson et al. 2023). For each topic pair and each study, the co-occurrence score was calculated as the proportion of shared email assignments relative to the smaller of the two topics’ email counts within that study. Co-occurrence scores range from 0 (no co-occurrence) to 1 (complete overlap), with higher values indicating topics that are more likely to appear together within the same emails.

title: Revealing the administrative process of data sharing: LLM-assisted topic modelling of COVID-19 Immunity Task Force Databank operations
text:
Topic Distribution Across Lifecycle Phases
[18] This analysis is based on 6,110 emails (89.4% of the full corpus) across 93 studies. From the full corpus we removed 7 studies with non-sequential milestone dates, then excluded emails sent before a study’s earliest milestone and after its publication milestone, leaving correspondence that falls within the project lifecycle. Emails were assigned to the phase in which they were sent, defined by consecutive project milestones, and the open-ended post-publication period was excluded, leaving five phases (Funding to Intro, Intro to DSA, DSA to Upload, Upload to Catalogue, Catalogue to Publication). For each study and phase we computed the share of that phase’s correspondence attributable to each topic, and reported the per-study median across studies. In Figure 4, each cell shows this per-study median share at a 15% topic-probability threshold, shaded white-to-color in proportion to its value, with a bordered cell marking each topic’s peak phase; rows are ordered top-to-bottom by peak phase, producing the early-to-late progression across the grid, and topics are colored by thematic category (Agreements and Contracts, Data Operations, Study Documentation, Coordination). To summarize how unevenly each topic was distributed across phases, we also computed, for each topic, the median across studies of the within-study standard deviation of its phase shares; higher values indicate topics whose correspondence concentrates in particular phases, and lower values indicate topics spread evenly across the lifecycle. These values appear in the rightmost column of Figure 4. Cells with fewer than five emails in a phase were omitted. The duration table (Table 1) is computed on the same 93-study sample using the same phase definitions, though its per-transition counts are smaller because a duration can only be measured for studies that reached both bounding milestones. All shares describe correspondence as observed from the Secretariat’s vantage point and should be read relative to this corpus rather than as absolute measures of project activity.






Figure 4: Per-study median topic share across project phases, by topic and lifecycle phase.



[19] Topic emphasis shifted systematically across the lifecycle, and the direction of that shift tracked thematic content (Figure 4). Agreements and Contracts topics were most prominent in the early phases. Agreement Drafting and Revisions (T8), Data Sharing Agreements and Governance (T0), DSA Status and Amendments (T5), and Agreement Signing and Execution (T7) all reached their highest per-study median share during Intro to DSA (26, 20, 19, and 13% respectively), while Document Review and Approval (T12) peaked one phase earlier, at Funding to Intro (22%). Data Operations topics became prominent progressively later and in sequence: Data Transfer Initiation (T10) was highest during DSA to Upload (29%), Variable Mapping and Schema Alignment (T3) and Data Upload Instructions and Credentials (T2) during Upload to Catalogue (29 and 33%), and Serology and Data Harmonization (T4) latest of all, reaching a median share of 55% during Catalogue to Publication, the highest per-study median of any topic in any phase.
[20] Topics differed not only in where they peaked but in how sharply, and this degree of phase-concentration was itself patterned by theme (rightmost column, Figure 4). The substantive and procedural topics were the most phase-concentrated, rising steeply in one or two phases and falling away elsewhere. Serology and Data Harmonization (T4) was the most concentrated of all (within-study SD of 19.0 percentage points), confined almost entirely to the final phase, followed by Agreement Drafting and Revisions (T8, 14.9) and Data Sharing Agreements and Governance (T0, 13.7), both confined to the negotiation phases. At the opposite extreme, the Coordination topics were nearly phase-invariant, maintaining a low-level presence across the entire lifecycle rather than peaking. Executive Correspondence (T6) held a median share near 5 to 6% across the early phases (SD 5.2, the lowest of any topic), and Meeting Scheduling and Invitations (T11) stayed close to 10 to 14% throughout (SD 8.3). This contrast is interpretable, since phase-concentrated topics correspond to discrete tasks tied to specific milestones, whereas the diffuse coordination topics reflect cross-cutting activities that recur whenever work is underway.
[21] Two further observations qualify the broad early-to-late shift. First, within Study Documentation the descriptive topics were prominent early while the more technical one was more evenly spread. Catalogue Onboarding and Collaboration (T9) and Study Description and Catalogue Publication (T1) were highest at Funding to Intro (26 and 20%), consistent with manual inspection showing that T9 captures the early correspondence through which studies are introduced to the Maelstrom catalogue rather than late-stage completion reminders, whereas Data Dictionary and Metadata (T13) remained relatively even across all five phases (median shares of 9 to 17%). Second, the Agreements and Contracts theme comprised four topics (T0, T5, T7, T8) that shared near-identical agreement-related subject lines but were separated by the model on the basis of email body content into distinct stages of the agreement lifecycle: establishing and governing the agreement (T0), drafting and revising it (T8), tracking its status and amendments (T5), and signing and executing it (T7). These topics co-occurred densely yet captured recognizably different correspondence, and Agreements concerns did not recede once formal agreements were executed; several retained appreciable median shares beyond the negotiation phases, suggesting that contractual and administrative attention persisted across the lifecycle rather than terminating at a single milestone.
[22] These communication patterns played out over uneven timescales (Table 1). Among studies that reached both bounding milestones, the negotiation phase (Intro to DSA) and the data preparation phase (DSA to Upload) had the longest median durations (395 and 397 days), while technical cataloguing (Upload to Catalogue) was much shorter (22 days). The phases in which agreements and data-operations correspondence concentrated were therefore also among the longest, so the thematic shift unfolded over extended periods of negotiation and preparation rather than at an even pace. Because durations are computed only for studies reaching both bounding milestones, later-phase estimates exclude studies that had not progressed that far and may understate typical times.

title: Revealing the administrative process of data sharing: LLM-assisted topic modelling of COVID-19 Immunity Task Force Databank operations
text:
Topic Distribution Across Sender Roles
[23] This analysis is based on 6,789 emails (99.4% of the full corpus) across 100 studies and 488 unique senders, after dropping a residual “Other” category covering 44 emails from three senders not assignable to one of the five operational roles. Unlike the phase analysis, no milestone filter was applied, because sender role is independent of a study’s timeline. The five roles comprised the Databank Secretariat (3,624 emails from 36 senders, the central coordination and administrative staff responsible for managing day-to-day operations, tracking milestones, and overseeing agreements), Study Staff (1,567 emails from 274 senders, research coordinators and data managers handling preparation and upload), Study Investigators (609 emails from 111 senders, principal and co-investigators responsible for governance decisions), External Partners (527 emails from 73 senders, including Statistics Canada, legal counsel, and government agencies), and the Databank Harmonization Group (462 emails from 4 senders, the specialized research team responsible for variable mapping and ensuring interoperability). For each topic, we computed per-(study, role) the share of that role’s correspondence to a study that was attributable to the topic, and report the per-study median across studies. In Figure 5, each cell shows this per-study median share at a 15% topic-probability threshold, shaded white-to-color in proportion to its value, with a bordered cell marking each topic’s peak role; rows are ordered top-to-bottom by peak role, grouping topics under the role that owns them, and topics are colored by thematic category (Agreements and Contracts, Data Operations, Study Documentation, Coordination). To summarize how unevenly each topic was distributed across roles, we computed, for each topic, the median across studies of the within-study standard deviation of its role shares; higher values indicate topics concentrated in one or a few roles, lower values indicate topics distributed evenly across roles. These values appear in the rightmost column of Figure 5. Cells with fewer than five emails in a role were omitted. Per-study medians vary in their basis across roles. The Secretariat contributed substantive correspondence to 88 studies, Study Staff to 63, the Harmonization Group to 48, Study Investigators to 42, and External Partners to only 22, reflecting that the two specialist roles were substantive correspondents in only a subset of studies. These per-role study counts appear in the bottom row of Figure 5.






Figure 5: Per-study median topic share across sender roles, with within-study SD column showing role-concentration.



[24] The five sender roles exhibited markedly distinct topical profiles, with three roles owning recognizably different territory and two filling more general coordinating functions (Figure 5). External Partners were the most contractually specialized. In the 22 studies in which they were substantive correspondents, agreement-related topics dominated their mail, with Agreement Signing and Execution (T7) reaching a per-study median share of 44% (the highest contractual concentration of any role), and Agreement Drafting and Revisions (T8), Data Sharing Agreements and Governance (T0), and DSA Status and Amendments (T5) reaching 33, 29, and 22% respectively. External Partners were near-absent from Data Operations and Study Documentation topics, with median shares of zero for variable mapping, serology and data harmonization, and dictionary work. The Databank Harmonization Group was the most documentation-specialized. Among the 48 studies for which it was a substantive correspondent, Study Description and Catalogue Publication (T1) reached a per-study median share of 48% (the highest single value of any role on any topic), followed by Data Dictionary and Metadata (T13) at 38% and Catalogue Onboarding and Collaboration (T9) at 29%. The Harmonization Group was at or near zero for every Agreements topic and for most Data Operations topics, indicating a tightly scoped role focused on cataloguing and metadata curation. Study Staff anchored the technical data-operations workstream, peaking on Data Upload Instructions and Credentials (T2, 13%) and Data Transfer Initiation (T10, 13%), the two topics most closely tied to the mechanics of moving and ingesting data. Study Investigators peaked on Meeting Scheduling and Invitations (T11, 20%), consistent with their governance role being enacted largely through meetings rather than through direct contractual or technical correspondence.
[25] The Databank Secretariat presented the most distinctive pattern. It appeared as the median peak for only two topics, Serology and Data Harmonization (T4, 17%) and Variable Mapping and Schema Alignment (T3, 15%), and instead held moderate shares across virtually every topic in the grid, ranging from 5 to 20%. This breadth is consistent with the Secretariat’s central coordinating mandate. It functioned as connective tissue, present in every workstream rather than owning any single one. This broad presence should be interpreted with the data source in mind: because the corpus is drawn from a Secretariat coordinator’s inbox, the Secretariat appears in every workstream partly by construction, since an email enters the corpus only by passing through this role. The per-study median guards against the Secretariat’s volume dominating the topic shares, but it cannot show how broad the Secretariat’s reach would look from another vantage point. This distribution also exposes a substantive difference between the per-study median and the pooled share. Pooled across emails, the Secretariat appeared to dominate several agreement topics simply because a small number of Secretariat individuals were extremely high-volume correspondents in this inbox; but within a typical study, External Partners or the Harmonization Group held the highest per-study median share on the topics where they specialized. The per-study median therefore credits coordinated workstream concentration rather than absolute volume in the inbox.
[26] The within-study standard deviation column quantifies how unevenly each topic was distributed across roles (Figure 5, right). Three topics stood out as the most role-specialized, namely Study Description and Catalogue Publication (T1, SD = 12.3 percentage points), Catalogue Onboarding and Collaboration (T9, SD = 10.2), and Data Dictionary and Metadata (T13, SD = 9.7). All three are Study Documentation topics owned by the Harmonization Group, indicating that catalogue and metadata work was the most narrowly scoped activity in the corpus. At the opposite extreme, Executive Correspondence (T6) was the least role-specialized of all 14 topics (SD = 5.1), confirming its character as cross-cutting institutional communication rather than the work of any specific role. The four Agreements and Contracts topics showed intermediate concentration (SDs of 8.4 to 9.0), reflecting that although External Partners peaked highest on these topics, contractual work was nonetheless distributed across multiple roles (Secretariat, Investigators, and Staff all maintained appreciable shares) rather than being owned by external parties exclusively.
[27] The External Partner and Harmonization Group columns rest on smaller study counts (22 and 48 respectively) because these roles were substantive correspondents in only a subset of studies. A research-team review of these studies indicated that they differ structurally from the rest. Studies in which External Partners were substantive correspondents had substantially higher overall email volume than studies without such correspondence (median 90.5 versus 53.5 emails), though they were no more likely to reach publication or progress further through the lifecycle. External involvement was thus associated with higher-volume studies rather than with a particular outcome. Studies in which the Harmonization Group was a substantive correspondent had progressed further through the lifecycle, reaching more milestones and twice the publication rate of studies without such correspondence (40 versus 20%), consistent with harmonization being a late-stage activity. The same review showed that the two specialist roles served largely non-overlapping sets of studies. Only 9 studies had substantive correspondence from both External Partners and the Harmonization Group, while 39 studies had neither. This pattern suggests that specialist involvement arose through two largely separate channels, legal-contractual on the one hand and technical-harmonization on the other, rather than a single population of complex studies attracting all specialists.

title: Revealing the administrative process of data sharing: LLM-assisted topic modelling of COVID-19 Immunity Task Force Databank operations
text:
Gender Distribution of Coordination Labour
[28] The gender analysis is based on 6,545 emails (95.8% of the full corpus) across 100 studies, after excluding senders whose gender could not be classified. Across the 455 unique gender-coded senders, women outnumbered men roughly two to one (294 women, 64.6%; 161 men, 35.4%). This imbalance was consistent at the study level. Of 100 studies, 70 had a majority-women sender base and only 18 had a majority-men sender base (median 60.0% women senders per study). The 64.6% women share of unique senders provides the corpus-wide baseline against which per-topic deviations should be read. A topic whose gender mix matches this baseline reflects the underlying composition of the sender base rather than a topic-specific gender pattern. Women sent a smaller share of emails than their headcount would imply (54.0% of gender-coded emails despite being 64.6% of senders), reflecting that women were on average lower-volume correspondents. We benchmark per-topic women-shares against the 64.6% sender baseline rather than the 54.0% email baseline so that deviations measure topic-level sorting relative to the available sender base, not differences in individual email volume.
[29] Individual breadth of involvement was nearly identical across genders. Both women and men engaged with a median of 5 distinct topics, and roughly half of each group (50.7% of women, 52.8% of men) engaged with five or more topics. A research-team review of multi-topic senders showed that the topics most frequently engaged with together were the same in both groups, involving combinations of Meeting Scheduling and Invitations (T11), Document Review and Approval (T12), and Catalogue Onboarding and Collaboration (T9). These topics, all of which sit near or at the corpus baseline in their gender distribution (Figure 6), functioned as the connective tissue of multi-topic coordination work. The gender differences visible in the corpus therefore reflect not whether women and men did multi-faceted coordination work, but which specific topics each group disproportionately handled.
[30] To make those topic-specific differences visible, we computed for each topic the per-study median share of its correspondence attributable to women. This framing lets each topic’s deviation from the 64.6% corpus baseline be read directly. Figure 6 displays these per-study medians at a 15% topic-probability threshold, sorted from most men-skewed at top to most women-skewed at bottom, with the corpus-wide women-share baseline (64.6%) shown as a dashed reference line. Bars are split into the women-share (light grey, left) and the complementary men-share (dark grey, right), with values summing to 100% of gender-coded correspondence on the topic. Per-topic values and the number of contributing studies (n = studies with ≥5 gender-coded emails on the topic) appear in the right margin, and topics are colored by thematic category (Agreements and Contracts, Data Operations, Study Documentation, Coordination). Cells with fewer than five gender-coded emails on a topic were omitted.






Figure 6: Per-study median women-share of topic correspondence, with corpus-wide women-share baseline shown as a dashed reference line.



[31] The most striking signal in the figure is the cluster of men-skewed Data Operations topics at the top. Serology and Data Harmonization (T4) had a per-study median women-share of 28.6%, 36 percentage points below the corpus baseline and the largest gender deviation in the corpus. Data Transfer Initiation (T10) and Data Upload Instructions and Credentials (T2) followed at 36.8 and 40.0% women-share, 27.8 and 24.6 percentage points below baseline respectively. Variable Mapping and Schema Alignment (T3), the remaining Data Operations topic, sat at 51.8% (12.8 percentage points below baseline). The full Data Operations theme therefore tilted toward men, with every topic substantially below the corpus baseline and the most technical pipeline work (serology, data transfer, upload) the most strongly men-skewed.
[32] Agreements and Contracts topics sat closer to the corpus baseline than to either pole. Three of the five (T0 at 50.8%, T5 at 51.8%, and T12 at 57.1% women) were at or above 50% women, while Agreement Drafting and Revisions (T8) at 46.2% and Agreement Signing and Execution (T7) at 47.7% dipped modestly below. Deviations from baseline ranged from 7.5 to 18.5 percentage points below, substantially smaller than the 25 to 36 point deviations seen in the technical pipeline topics. The pooled email-level view obscured even this milder pattern by showing several of these topics as gender-balanced; the per-study median makes the modest skew visible, but contractual work was not strongly gendered in the way the technical pipeline work was.
[33] By contrast, women’s over-representation was concentrated in Study Documentation and was smaller in magnitude than men’s over-representation in the technical pipeline work. Data Dictionary and Metadata (T13) reached 71.8% women (7.2 percentage points above baseline), Study Description and Catalogue Publication (T1) reached 71.4% (6.8 above), and Executive Correspondence (T6) also reached 71.4% (6.8 above), though this last estimate rests on a smaller study count (n = 32) and the topic is also the least coherent in the NMF (c_v = 0.473), so its women-skew should be read cautiously. Catalogue Onboarding and Collaboration (T9) and Meeting Scheduling and Invitations (T11), the two remaining topics in the corpus, both sat at or near baseline (0.6 and -2.1 percentage points respectively) and represent activities for which gender mix matched the underlying sender-base composition.
[34] The overall pattern resolved into three tiers rather than two. Men were strongly over-represented in the technical pipeline work that moved data through the system (Data Operations topics, 25 to 36 percentage points below the women-majority baseline), women were over-represented in the documentation and metadata work that described it (Study Documentation topics, around 7 percentage points above baseline), and the contractual work that authorized the data sharing (Agreements and Contracts topics) sat closer to the sender baseline, with mild deviations spanning both sides of 50% women. The gender pattern therefore tracked a technical-versus-descriptive axis more cleanly than it tracked the agreements-versus-data-operations split visible in the phase, role, and co-occurrence analyses. These figures describe correspondents to a single coordinator’s inbox rather than the initiative’s workforce as a whole, and because the technical pipeline topics were anchored by Study Staff and the Harmonization Group, the men-skew of these topics may reflect the gender composition of the roles that handled them rather than gendered sorting of work within roles. Despite making up nearly two-thirds of the gender-coded sender base, women were under-represented among correspondents on the technical pipeline work and over-represented on the documentation and metadata work, a division consistent with prior research on the gendered division of professional work, including accounts of the feminization of coordination labour in research data infrastructure (Choroszewicz 2022), though the present data measure correspondence shares only and cannot speak to whether this work was recognized, credited, or valued.

title: Revealing the administrative process of data sharing: LLM-assisted topic modelling of COVID-19 Immunity Task Force Databank operations
text:
Co-occurrence Analysis of Topic Relationships
[35] This analysis is based on the full corpus of 6,833 emails across 100 studies, examining how often pairs of topics were assigned to the same email within a study’s correspondence. For each topic pair and each study, we computed the co-occurrence score as the number of emails assigned to both topics divided by the smaller of the two topics’ total email counts in that study (Stevenson et al. 2023), and report the median across studies. In Figure 7, each cell shows this per-study median co-occurrence score at a 15% topic-probability threshold, with circle area proportional to the score and cells in the 0–5% range collapsed into a uniform small-circle bin so that low-coupling cells render as visible markers rather than disappearing entirely. Rows and columns are grouped by thematic category, with topics ordered within each theme by ascending email count, and topics are colored by thematic category (Agreements and Contracts, Data Operations, Study Documentation, Coordination). The bottom row reports the total emails per topic via multi-topic assignment.






Figure 7: Per-study median co-occurrence of topic pairs within studies, with circle size proportional to the score.



[36] Within typical studies, two largely separate topical clusters emerged from the corpus, with limited coupling between them (Figure 7). The first comprised five Agreements and Contracts topics that travelled together within studies, with the highest within-cluster pairs being Agreement Signing and Execution × Agreement Drafting and Revisions (T7 × T8, 33.3%), Agreement Drafting and Revisions × Document Review and Approval (T8 × T12, 32.1%), Data Sharing Agreements and Governance × Agreement Drafting and Revisions (T0 × T8, 28.6%), Data Sharing Agreements and Governance × DSA Status and Amendments (T0 × T5, 28.6%), and DSA Status and Amendments × Agreement Drafting and Revisions (T5 × T8, 25.0%). Within a typical study’s correspondence, roughly a quarter to a third of emails on any one of these topics also touched another. The second cluster combined Data Operations with Study Documentation topics, with the highest pairs being Variable Mapping and Schema Alignment × Data Dictionary and Metadata (T3 × T13, 35.3%, the largest within-study coupling in the corpus), Variable Mapping and Schema Alignment × Serology and Data Harmonization (T3 × T4, 33.3%), Study Description and Catalogue Publication × Serology and Data Harmonization (T1 × T4, 29.5%), and Serology and Data Harmonization × Data Dictionary and Metadata (T4 × T13, 20.0%). The technical work of mapping variables, harmonizing serology data, documenting metadata, and describing studies for the catalogue therefore moved together within studies as a single integrated workstream that crossed the Data Operations and Study Documentation themes.
[37] The two clusters showed minimal within-study coupling with each other. Pairs spanning Agreements topics and Data Operations topics, or Agreements and Study Documentation, mostly fell in the 0–5% range (Figure 7), indicating that within a typical study, contractual work and technical data work did not regularly appear in the same emails. The pooled, corpus-level view of the same data suggested moderate cross-cluster coupling (5 to 12%) for many such pairs, but the per-study median shows that these apparent connections were diffuse cross-corpus artifacts rather than features of typical study workflows. This reading rests on the assumption that integration between the two workstreams, had it occurred, would have surfaced in correspondence reaching this coordinator; cross-workstream exchanges conducted between other parties, or outside email altogether, would not register as co-occurrence here. The Agreements cluster and the Data Operations and Study Documentation cluster were therefore parallel workstreams within the observed correspondence, paralleling the temporal sequencing observed in the phase analysis, the role specialization observed in the sender analysis, and the gendered division of labour observed in the gender analysis.
[38] The connectivity profile of individual topics, computed as the mean of each topic’s co-occurrence with the other thirteen across studies, revealed which activities were most and least integrated with the rest of the work. The most connected topic was Serology and Data Harmonization (T4, mean within-study co-occurrence 14.0%), reflecting that serology work involved coordinating with variable mapping, dictionary curation, and study description simultaneously. The least connected topic was Executive Correspondence (T6, 5.3%), which had appeared moderately connected in the pooled corpus-level view but proved to be a diffuse cross-cutting topic with little within-study integration. Data Upload Instructions and Credentials (T2, 6.8%) was similarly isolated, consistent with upload being a narrow technical task that occurred at one specific point in the lifecycle and was anchored by a specific role, as shown in the phase and sender analyses.
[39] The within-study coupling between Variable Mapping and Schema Alignment (T3) and Data Dictionary and Metadata (T13) was the strongest single coupling in the corpus and is worth noting separately. These two topics, despite belonging to different themes (Data Operations and Study Documentation), are connected by the workflow that links technical schema work to the descriptive metadata that documents it. A research-team review of T3 × T13 emails confirmed that this coupling reflects the parallel production of variable mappings and data dictionaries, since the same exchanges that established how variables would be harmonized produced the metadata describing them. This is a cross-theme integration that the theme structure obscures but the within-study coupling reveals.

title: Shifting to supervised topic assignment
text:
Note



I wrote this document in September 2026, after an informal consultation on how to code the emails, and revised it alongside the mockup through October 22. The restructuring plan has since superseded it. The plan codes rhetoric, functions and actions as three kinds of codes, and starts coding without a codebook.
The shift replaces NMF topic assignment at a 15% threshold with human coding of passages. A coder selects a passage of newly written content in a purpose-built page and gives it one topic code. An email has no topic codes of its own, and the analysis phase derives its topics from its coded passages. Coders code a sample of 100 to 200 emails from the pilot corpus this way, and those codes guide and validate a local model that applies them to the full corpus. The pilot’s four themes carry over as categories of the codebook, alongside an Other category.

title: Shifting to supervised topic assignment
text:
Arguments for the shift

1. Fixed categories let the expanded corpus test the pilot
The protocol describes the pilot as a pipeline test that produced preliminary observations, and the expansion to the Scientific Director’s and data managers’ mailboxes exists to find out whether those observations hold at scale. Refitting NMF on a corpus with different senders and a different vocabulary yields a new solution with its own k and its own topic labels, so a pilot topic such as Serology and Data Harmonization has no guarantee of reappearing. A comparison across the two corpora would then compare two different sets of categories. Supervised codes hold the categories constant, so the expanded corpus can retest, on the same constructs, the finding that agreements work and data operations work ran as parallel workstreams.
NMF stays in the methods as the exploratory stage that generated the category scheme, and the codes do not guide its fitting. Its dominant-topic assignments stratify the annotation sample so that it includes rare categories, and agreement between each email’s dominant NMF topic and its dominant coded theme reports how much of the pilot’s structure the coded labels reproduce. Because the codes did not shape the topics, that agreement is evidence.


2. Human labels supply validity evidence that coherence scores cannot
The c_v score measures whether a topic’s top words co-occur. It says nothing about whether a topic corresponds to a type of administrative work. The two least coherent topics, Meeting Scheduling and Invitations (0.473) and Executive Correspondence (0.497), make up the entire Coordination theme, whose generic language the codebook has to define most carefully. The LLM-generated labels also needed correction by hand. The application and the protocol label one topic Catalogue Completion Reminders; the preprint relabels it Catalogue Onboarding and Collaboration after manual inspection showed it captures early introductions to the Maelstrom catalogue. Five of the 14 labels differ between the protocol’s Table 1 and the preprint. A label attached after the fact is a hypothesis about what a word cluster means, and every downstream analysis treats it as a measurement.
A supervised design reports validity as coder agreement on the double-coded sample and as precision and recall for each theme against the human codes.


3. The 15% threshold measures vocabulary mix
A weight threshold on a normalized NMF matrix records how an email’s vocabulary divides across topics. In the pilot, 72.7% of emails cleared 15% on two or more topics (mean 2.01 per email). Four of the Agreements topics (T0, T5, T7, T8) share near-identical subject lines and separate on body vocabulary. The preprint reads them as stages of the agreement lifecycle, and that reading carries weight because four of the cluster’s five most strongly coupled pairs (25 to 33%) are among them. The model cannot tell a change in activity from a change in wording, so the reading remains an interpretation. Coding tests it. Annotators either distinguish the stages reliably or they do not, and reliability is reportable.
The threshold is also a free parameter. The protocol weighed 10%, 15%, and 20%, and every phase, role, gender, and co-occurrence result inherits the choice. A coder deciding which topic a passage carries replaces the threshold with a judgment that the team can document and check for reliability, and an email’s split across topics follows from where each topic appears in its text.


4. Passage codes restore single counts and record where topics arise
Under the threshold scheme an email appears in every topic cell it clears, so the cells in the phase, role, and gender figures overlap. The application specified a simpler design in which, for the workflow phase and sender analyses, “emails will be assigned to their dominant topic”, with the multi-topic threshold reserved for co-occurrence. The preprint applied the 15% threshold to every analysis.
Passage coding restores the application’s design. Each passage takes one topic, and an email’s profile is the share of its coded words in each theme, with word count as the weight because it is the only quantity a coder’s decision directly produces. Each email counts once in the phase, role, gender, and network analyses, with its count divided across themes in proportion to those shares, and the theme with the largest share supplies the dominant topic that the application specified. The profile has no cap, so the 25.1% of pilot emails that carried three or more topics keep every topic. Co-occurrence describes the themes that appear together in an email, and the position of each passage also records which topic arises first. Because a coder assigns each topic to a stretch of text, the profile reflects what the email does in its own words, in units that sum to the email’s coded length.


5. One coded construct serves the topic, network, and questionnaire analyses
A single paper needs one unit of analysis across its topic and network sections, and the coded email is that unit. With network analysis folded in, topic labels become attributes of edges. In the person projection each edge inherits the topics of the emails exchanged, and at 2.01 topics per email those inherited labels are overlapping sets, which complicates claims about which topics carry bridging ties, such as data managers linking study teams to the Harmonization Group on Data Operations. The derived profile gives each email a weight of one divided across themes, so an edge’s topic profile is a distribution over themes that sums to one.
In the email co-participation projection, nodes that carry several topics tie topics together through the labels themselves as well as through shared people, which blurs the line between that projection and the co-occurrence analysis. Labelling each node with its dominant theme restores the line, with co-occurrence describing content through passage-level topics and the projection describing people.
The codebook’s role categories supply node attributes with definitions fixed in advance. The four exclusion flags give the protocol’s exclusion of systemic notification traffic a coded basis that the analysis can report and audit.
The questionnaire’s second and third domains correspond to the email analysis’s topic and phase categories, and its thematic coding starts from the email analysis framework. Defined codes with inclusion rules move into that coding intact. An NMF topic moves as a list of keywords.


6. A local model already in the pipeline scales the codes
Manual annotation covers a sample of 100 to 200 emails from the pilot corpus, and a local model applies the codes to the remaining emails and to the expanded corpus, which grows well beyond the pilot’s 6,833 emails. The pipeline already runs Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on secure servers to label topics, so few-shot prompting with annotated examples extends existing infrastructure and keeps email content on McGill servers. A sample of this size supports prompting and validation, and the codebook’s anchor examples serve as the few-shot examples, so annotators and model work from one artefact. Passage-level codes also give the model the exact text behind each code. The annotation itself is qualitative coding, the competence the questionnaire analysis also requires, and it follows the process used for the BibVik codebook.

title: Shifting to supervised topic assignment
text:
Objections and responses
The first three objections are serious. The design handles the rest.

1. The codebook inherits the pilot’s structure, so confirmation is partly circular
The top-level categories are the pilot’s four themes and the example codes come from its topics. Coders applying those definitions will tend to sort emails as the topic model did, so the design partly builds in agreement with the pilot’s findings. A fixed codebook also cannot show what the pilot missed. The annotated sample comes from the operations manager’s mailbox, so the validation covers that mailbox only, and the Scientific Director’s mailbox will carry governance and leadership correspondence the sample never covered.
Response. Add an Other category for substantive passages that fit no theme, review the passages coded into it after annotation, and version the codebook with dated changes. Annotate a further small sample from each added mailbox before applying the codes to it. Fit NMF to the expanded corpus as well and report any topic that no code accounts for. Discovery stays in the design, and the confirmatory claims rest on categories that could change.


2. The threshold and single-count arguments do not require supervision
An unsupervised design can fix the overlap problem. The application already specifies dominant-topic assignment for phase and sender analyses, and a threshold sensitivity analysis, a lower k, or merging the four Agreements topics would address the rest. A reviewer can accept everything said about the 15% threshold and about single counting and still ask why humans need to label anything. Fixed categories, validity evidence, defined codes shared with the questionnaire and the network roles, and local classification are the arguments that justify supervision itself.
Response. Lead the justification with fixed categories and validity evidence, and present the single count and the record of where topics arise as additional benefits of coding.


3. A sample of 100 to 200 emails cannot support fine-grained claims
The codebook lists example codes under four themes and an Other category, and the full set will be larger. Spread across 100 to 200 emails, rare codes receive a handful of examples or none, so per-code precision and recall are unstable. A proportion estimated on 100 to 200 emails carries a 95% interval of about 7 to 10 percentage points at its widest. Fine-tuning a classifier on this few labels is out of reach, and few-shot prompting is the workable route. The main analyses also report per-study medians and drop cells with fewer than five emails, so misclassification in rare codes moves results more than it would in pooled counts. LLM output varies with temperature and seed, and the pilot already ran its LLM tasks across five temperature settings to check stability.
Response. Make the four themes the validated classification targets and keep the finer codes as descriptive annotation. Report agreement and per-theme precision and recall with bootstrap confidence intervals. Run the model at temperature 0 with fixed seeds and limit claims to themes that meet a stated performance floor. Propagate the confusion matrix into the main results by resampling assigned labels, and report how far the headline findings move.


4. Passage-level codes have no reliability record
Agreement on passages needs coders to agree on which stretches of text carry a topic, where each stretch begins and ends, and which topic it carries. Two coders can choose the same code for slightly different stretches, split one stretch into two passages, or leave a stretch uncoded that the other codes. A single topic per passage removes the disagreement over which of several codes applies and adds a disagreement over where to split. The pilot’s human review rested mostly on one research assistant. A sample of 100 to 200 makes double-coding feasible, which removes most of the capacity problem.
Response. Double-code the whole sample and adjudicate disagreements. Measure agreement in three places. For the derived email profiles, use Krippendorff’s alpha on each email’s dominant theme, with 0.67 as the floor for tentative conclusions and 0.80 for firm ones. For passages, count two coders’ passages as the same when they overlap on more than half their words, report the share of passages matched, and report alpha for the code assigned to matched passages against the same floors. Because passage length is the profile’s weight, also report the difference in word count between the two coders’ versions of each matched passage, since two coders can agree on a passage and its topic while disagreeing on its length by enough to move the email’s profile. Selections snap to whole words, which removes the commonest source of that difference. Since the model must also find passages, evaluate it at the sentence level by projecting human passages onto sentences. If passage agreement fails and email-level agreement holds, analyze at the email level using derived profiles alone. If both fail, keep NMF with dominant-topic assignment.


5. A single topic per passage forces a choice
Emails often do several things in one sentence, such as returning a signed agreement and proposing a call. A single topic per passage forces the coder to split the sentence or to drop one of the topics, and either choice loses information that the threshold scheme kept as overlap.
The constraint follows from the weighting. Passage length is the profile’s weight, and each word counts once, toward the theme of its passage. A passage carrying two topics would need its length counted toward each, which inflates the email’s total past its coded length, or a further rule to split its length between them, which brings back a ranked judgment under the name of a topic assignment. A single topic per passage keeps the weighting well defined, so an email’s coded length divides across themes with no remainder and no word counted twice.
Response. Write a splitting rule into the codebook. Code at the level of the clause where possible, and where one clause carries two topics, code the topic the sender asks the recipient to act on, or the main information the email conveys when it requests nothing, and start a new passage for the other. Report the share of passages coders mark unsure, and run the main results without them as a check.


6. Creating codes while coding erodes the codebook
Coders can create a code from the selection when no existing code fits. Each new code changes the codebook mid-round, so emails coded earlier never had the chance to receive it, and two coders can create overlapping codes for the same thing. Free creation is also the quickest route to a codebook that drifts from its definitions.
Response. Allow creation only during calibration. A code created on the fly is provisional, records the email it came from, and stays undefined until a coder writes a definition in the codebook drawer. The team reviews provisional codes after each calibration round, merges duplicates, and recodes affected passages before the codebook freezes. Once it freezes, the create option turns off, and a coder who finds a gap codes the passage in the Other category.


7. The codes could guide the topic model directly
Seeding or regularizing NMF with the codebook, or fitting a guided model to the annotated emails, would put the codes to work on the topics themselves. A sample of 100 to 200 emails is too small to supervise a factorization across 14 or more topics. Guidance also makes the topics reflect the codebook. Agreement between NMF and the human codes then becomes partly built in, a fresh NMF on the expanded corpus loses its value as a check on what the codebook misses, and something the codebook produced replaces the pilot’s unsupervised results.
Response. Keep NMF unguided and use the codes to evaluate it. Report agreement between each email’s dominant NMF topic and its dominant coded theme, weigh it alongside c_v when comparing k and stopword choices, choose those on one split of the sample, and report final agreement on the held-out split. Fit a fresh NMF to the passages coded in the Other category, and treat topics that surface there as candidates for new codes. Other serves as the intake point for the codebook’s next revision.


8. Dropping actions loses the record of what an email asks for
An earlier draft of the codebook coded actions such as request, provide, chase, confirm, and decide alongside topics. The intent was a relation that could sit between a topic and the party it concerned, moving toward a subject-predicate-object structure in which the action is the verb. That structure needs a well-formed object, such as what a request asks for or what a chase pursues. No part of the codebook identifies that object consistently, so coders coded the verb with nothing for it to attach to, and an action code alone cannot say what the sender requested or from whom. Retrofitting the object later, from role codes or from passage adjacency, would add to the codebook without drawing on anything the design already produces.
Response. Drop actions from the codebook, since a verb with no object adds a code without the information it was meant to carry. If the analysis later needs the coordination-versus-friction distinction that actions aimed to capture, design the object slot first, for example by linking a passage to the role codes of its sender and recipient, and add the verb once the codebook specifies the relation it completes.


9. The change departs from the application and the preprint
The application names NMF, its evaluation against three alternatives, and LLM-generated labels as the method, and the preprint reports NMF results. Dropping NMF as the primary method can read as abandoning the validated pipeline. The preprint also presents NMF with LLM annotation as a replicable approach other groups can adapt, whereas supervised coding asks each group to build a codebook for its own corpus.
Response. Keep NMF as the exploratory stage, record the change in the protocol with its rationale and date, and leave the preprint unchanged as the pilot record. Publish the codebook and annotation guidelines so the codebook becomes the transferable output.


10. Annotation widens human exposure to email content
Presidio as configured replaces names, email addresses, and URLs, so phone numbers and institutional and study details remain in the text. Annotators read each sampled email in full. The sample size of 100 to 200 keeps that exposure small, and the reading shows which identifying details de-identification missed.
Response. Coders flag any passage that contains identifying information, marking the passage whether or not it also carries a topic. The team redacts flagged passages before quoting or publishing them, and before using them as few-shot examples. The flag rate also audits the de-identification step. Confirm that the ethics file (REB #26-08-029) covers annotation by the research team, and annotate only cleaned, de-identified text on the secure servers, under the confidentiality terms that apply to the pipeline research assistant.

title: Shifting to supervised topic assignment
text:
Coding design
A mockup of the coding page, built with invented emails, shows the design this section describes.

Code from a selection
Coding happens on the fly. A coder selects a passage in the newly written content, and a popover opens beside it. The coder picks a category, which is one of the four themes or Other, and a search box lists that category’s existing codes and offers to create a new one when none matches. The passage takes that one code. The number keys pick a category, so the mouse stays in the text. Each coding carries its own unsure flag, and each passage carries its own flag for identifying information, which can stand alone on a passage that has no topic.
The interface keeps three levels apart. Passage codes attach to selected text and show as highlights coloured by category, with a wavy red underline for identifying information. Each email’s Flags section holds the email-level flags and the note. Roles belong to people, and coders set them in the review pane. When a passage already has a code, the popover shows it with a Remove button, and the review pane offers the same control along with the unsure and identifying-information checkboxes.
Passages do not overlap. Selections snap outward to whole words, and arrow buttons move either edge of a passage by one word, so a loose selection does not become a boundary disagreement.


Leave email-level topics to the analysis phase
Emails carry no topic codes of their own, and the coding page shows no email-level profile. The analysis phase derives the profile from the passages, which gives each email a single measurement of its topics that cannot disagree with them. The profile is each theme’s share of the email’s coded words, chosen because passage length is the only quantity a coder’s decision produces, and a one-word passage should not weigh as much as a paragraph. Coders code every substantive passage of newly written content and leave greetings, sign-offs, and quoted history uncoded, so the coded length reflects content and excludes message boilerplate. Recompute the profile from passage counts as a sensitivity check. Coders flag an email with no substantive content instead of coding it.


Separate topic from actor
The example codes mix subjects (Informed consent), activities (Cleaning, Uploading), and actors (Contracts officers, Research ethics boards). Contracts officer also appears as an Institutional role, so coders would code the same information twice. Topic codes cover activity and subject matter, and actors go to the role coding.


Define codes and fix the unit of coding
Each code gets a definition, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and two or three anchor examples, including a boundary case. Written rules cover the adjacent codes that coders will confuse, such as Schema / map / spreadsheet / variables against Data dictionary / metadata, Harmonization against Core data elements, and Data governance against Data sharing agreements. The pilot’s strongest cross-theme coupling was between variable mapping and the data dictionary, so that boundary gets its rule first. Coders code what the sender does in the newly written content of the email. They may see the prior message for context and ignore quoted history, so coders code a reply that quotes a long agreement thread for its own content.
Every code anchors to the passage that justifies it, and a passage takes one topic. The anchoring limits over-application, speeds adjudication, and allows a check on whether the model cites the same passages. The splitting rule in the codebook says where one passage ends and the next begins.


Add flags
Six flags carry what the codes do not. Four apply to an email in place of coding it, and exactly one of the four applies to a given email. Too short covers content too brief to code, such as a one-line acknowledgement. Delivery status notification covers a mailer-daemon or bounce message, Out of office an automatic vacation reply, and Automated notification any other system-generated message, such as a calendar invite or a platform alert. Pruning removes content-free emails from the sample before coding begins, so these flags catch what the pruning missed, and a high rate of use signals that the pruning step needs revisiting. Setting any of the four clears any passages already coded on that email, so a flagged email carries no orphaned codes and the flag is the complete record of why it was not coded. The analysis reports agreement on these email-level flags with the rest, and their counts alongside the coded corpus.
Two further flags apply to a passage or a coding, and neither constrains the other. Identifying information marks a passage that contains details de-identification missed. It can stand alone on a passage with no topic or sit alongside one, since the flag and the code record different things about the same text. Removing it from a passage with no code also removes the passage, because a passage exists only to hold a code, a flag, or both. Unsure marks a single coding that the coder doubts, since doubt attaches to a coding decision. Content that fits no theme takes a code in the Other category. A note field holds anything the second coder or adjudicator should know. The flags feed codebook revision, and the reliability analysis reports agreement with and without the unsure codings.


Code roles on the person, kept simple for round 1
Round 1 codes each person once per study from a single list of roles grouped by domain, chosen from a select box in the review pane, with the date the role applies from. A crosswalk from the pilot’s five sender roles to the codebook roles keeps pilot findings comparable. Point man becomes Point person, since gender is an analytic variable in this study. Automated services remains a role, and emails from it take one of the four exclusion flags, most often Automated notification.
Roles are the least settled part of the codebook. A role depends on the circumstances of an action and an interaction, and a title conflates it with position. A list of positions does not capture what a person did in a given exchange. Round 1 does not settle this. The disagreements coders show on roles decide afterward whether roles stay positional, become situated in the email or the interaction, or split into both. Coding people and institutions mentioned in the text waits on that decision.


Stage the process and keep the codebook as data
Coders code two calibration rounds of about 20 to 30 emails independently and discuss them, and those emails stay outside the sample. The team freezes the codebook version before the double-coded sample begins, and a dated changelog records later changes. Codes created on the fly during calibration stay provisional until reviewed, and creation turns off at the freeze. Annotators do not see NMF topics or model predictions, since those anchor judgments and undermine the independence of the NMF comparison. The sample uses a floor of about 25 emails per theme, with the theme taken from the NMF dominant topic, and a cap on emails per study so high-volume studies do not dominate. Coordination needs deliberate oversampling to reach that floor, since it is the smallest theme in the pilot, with about 1,600 topic assignments against about 3,800 for Agreements.
Codes, definitions, and examples live in a YAML file that renders into the qmd and feeds the coding page and the model prompt, so the three cannot drift apart. This matches the literate programming commitment in the protocol.

title: Shifting to supervised topic assignment
text:
Framing in the paper
Present the design as two stages within the email work package. NMF with LLM labelling is the exploratory stage that produced the category scheme from the pilot corpus. Hand coding of a 100 to 200 email sample is the confirmatory stage that fixes those categories, and agreement between the local model and the human codes validates the model’s labels at scale. NMF stays unguided by the codes, so the two stages remain independent checks on each other. The same codes then carry into the network and questionnaire analyses. The application names NMF as the method, so the change goes into the protocol as a documented refinement, with the pilot’s topic model retained as the comparison showing how much of its structure the coded labels reproduce.

title: Shifting to supervised topic assignment
text:
Recommendation
Run two calibration rounds on emails outside the sample, review the codes created on the fly, and freeze the codebook version. Then double-code the 100 to 200 email sample and treat its agreement thresholds as the go/no-go decision. If the sample meets them, apply the codes at the theme level with a few-shot local model that uses the codebook’s anchor examples and that the sample validates, keep the Other category, and refit NMF on the expanded corpus without guidance from the codes. If they are not met, keep NMF with dominant-topic assignment, which is the design the application already describes.

title: Relating rhetoric to functions
text:
Note



I wrote this document on November 13, 2026, following a comprehensive assessment of DocuScope for tagging the rhetoric of the CITF emails. The restructuring plan has since superseded this document, but its concerns about relating DocuScope tags to functional categories still stand. The plan’s section on relating rhetoric, functions and actions builds on them.
The project relates how people wrote (the how) to what their emails did (the what), with sender role and workflow phase as context. DocuScope supplies the how and nothing else. Functional coding supplies the what, through codes derived from the emails without an initial codebook and grouped into functional categories. The two streams stay separate until integration, so any association between them reflects the emails themselves.
Relating the two streams needs a method that first identifies the functional units of a text and then describes their language. Corpus-based move analysis does this. It fits the project for two reasons. It defines function before it examines language, as the functional coding does. It compares functional and linguistic analyses derived independently, which matches keeping the two streams separate. The project takes the sentence as its unit, since sentences need no hand segmentation. A sentence can carry several functional categories, and it counts in each.
The central analysis is the variation within each functional category, explained by role, phase and the relationship between sender and recipient, and read closely at prototypical and peripheral cases.

title: Relating rhetoric to functions
text:
2.1 Detecting rhetoric in fragments
A DocuScope tag in a sentence with a functional category shows only that the two co-occur. Take the follow-up “Sorry to bother you again, could you send a copy of the agreement we signed last week?” “Could you send” is the request itself. “Sorry” is an apology that softens the request. “The agreement we signed last week” recounts an earlier event. DocuScope may tag all three, but only the first two tags describe how the writer made the request.
We considered three ways of linking a tag to the act it describes, and set each aside. Linking each DocuScope tag to the verb that performs the request, through dependency parses, would rest on single tags, such as “sorry” in the follow-up above, and DocuScope is not designed for single-tag readings. Counting the tags in the sentences before and after each sentence would catch framing such as “I know you’re busy, but”, yet those sentences carry their own functional categories, so counting their tags twice would blur the comparison between categories. Linking a tag to a request when its clause stands in a marked relation to it, such as a condition (“if you have time”) or a concession, works only where connectives mark the relation, and again rests on single tags.
We therefore accept co-occurrence as the measure. Some tags in a sentence describe something other than its function, as “the agreement we signed last week” does in a request, and the comparison with the corpus absorbs them where they occur evenly across functional categories. Tags that cluster in one category, as accounts of earlier events may in follow-ups, need checking in the close reading before they count as its rhetoric.

title: Relating rhetoric to functions
text:
2.2 Defining and varying rhetoric
Some rhetoric defines a functional category, and some reflects how writers chose to frame the work. For example, nearly every request addresses the reader and asks for something, as in “could you send”, so that rhetoric belongs to the request itself. Whether the writer apologises, sets a deadline or explains the need varies from request to request, and that variation is the kind of choice worth tracking. DocuScope tags words independently of their functional context, and it is necessary to differentiate these two kinds of rhetoric.
Within each functional category, we separate rhetoric present in nearly every sentence from rhetoric that varies across sentences. For example, nearly every request addresses the reader, while only some apologise, set a deadline or explain the need. The varying part shows how writers chose to frame the work.

title: Relating rhetoric to functions
section: 2.3 Disentangling rhetoric’s relationship with role and function
text:
2.3 Disentangling rhetoric’s relationship with role and function
The rhetoric of a functional category may reflect who writes it. If CITF coordinators write most requests and study teams write most reports, a difference in rhetoric between requests and reports may come from the writers, from the work, or from the way a writer’s role shapes how they do the work. Distinguishing these depends on people who write in several functional categories, and such writers may be few.
We compare the same senders across functional categories, and model sender and study as random effects. For example, a coordinator who writes both requests and reports shows whether requests read differently from reports when the writer stays the same. If too few senders write in several functional categories, the random effects carry the comparison alone, and the analysis reports the confound as a limit.

title: DocuScope Assessment
text:
[1] The CITF email project studies research data sharing through the correspondence that carried it. A first close reading of 30 emails showed that how people wrote mattered as much as what they wrote about, and we adopted DocuScope, following Brown and Laudenbach (2022), to capture the how at corpus scale. The project uses DocuScope for HOW categories only.
[2] This session asked whether DocuScope’s HOW tags describe these emails accurately enough to support that use, and built a reproducible procedure to find tagging errors, measure them, and correct the ones that can be corrected. Every step that changes the data is code with fixed parameters, and every human judgement is stored as a coded file, so that each result can be rerun and audited.

title: DocuScope Assessment
text:
4.1 Excluding automated notifications
[12] Automated notifications have no author, so blocks 10 and 12 leave them out by sender. The run excluded 30 notifications from DocuSign, SharePoint and WeTransfer, leaving 6,056 emails and 174,765 HOW tags. The count is small because block 7’s filters already remove most notifications, and because the rule identifies automated emails by sender address alone. Automated messages sent from a person’s address therefore remain in the pool, including ticket confirmations (“Reference#: REF00000 Please use this number when inquiring”) and out-of-office replies. Catching them requires patterns on email content, such as “out of the office”, “absent du bureau” or “Reference#”, which no block includes yet.

title: DocuScope Assessment
text:
4.2 Zones
[13] An email body holds more than what its sender wrote for that message. It also carries earlier messages quoted below a reply, notices that mail systems insert, markup, signature blocks and boilerplate lines that recur across many emails. DocuScope tags all of this text alike, but tags in it describe other writers, mail software or standing institutional text, not the sender’s rhetoric. Because the same signatures and notices repeat word for word across hundreds of emails, their tags also make senders look more alike than their writing is. Blocks 9 and 10 therefore divide each email into zones and keep only the authored zone for analysis.
[14] Block 9 labels the email bodies with Chipmunk (Bevendorff et al. 2020), a neural model trained to segment emails. Chipmunk gives each line of an email body one of 15 labels, such as paragraph, closing, personal signature, quotation and mail client signature. The model runs on the CITF analysis server, so no email text leaves it.
[15] We chose Chipmunk after comparing the published tools for email zoning, the task of dividing an email into parts such as greeting, body, signature and quoted text (Lampert, Dale, and Paris 2009). Rule-based libraries such as talon, email_reply_parser and mail-parser-reply detect only quotations and signatures, and their authors report no evaluation. Zebra (Lampert, Dale, and Paris 2009) exists only in third-party reimplementations, and Chipmunk outperformed Quagga (Repke and Krestel 2018) in its authors’ tests. Chipmunk is peer-reviewed, its authors released its code, training data and trained model, and it labels greetings and closings and separates personal signatures from notices that mail programs add.
[16] We tested Chipmunk extensively before using it. Its authors trained it on Gmane, an archive of public mailing lists. They tested it on Gmane and on Enron, a corpus of corporate email. We reran both tests and reproduced their results (Zoning Tests). We also ran Chipmunk on five CITF emails and compared its zones with a provisional labelling made during testing, which has not been reviewed.
[17] We compared Chipmunk with Okapi (Jardim, Rei, and Almeida 2021). Okapi is a multilingual extension of Chipmunk that keeps its 15 zones and Gmane training emails. Chipmunk reads the layout of each line and the lines around it. Okapi reads the wording of each line through a multilingual language model. Okapi’s authors published its design but no trained model. We therefore built Okapi from their paper and trained it ourselves, and the Okapi results in the table come from our rebuild. The two models score alike on Gmane and Enron. On the five CITF emails Okapi labelled whole signature blocks as authored text in three of them and Chipmunk did not. The table gives the share of lines each model labels correctly. It also gives the results that Chipmunk’s authors report for Quagga and an SVM baseline on the same benchmarks.

[19] The tests also exposed one weakness, which the code in block 10 corrects. On Enron, Chipmunk and Okapi both read about a quarter of banner and disclaimer lines as authored text. Block 10 therefore adds the disclaimer rule and the banner regular expressions described below.
[20] Block 10 maps Chipmunk’s 15 line labels onto six zones. Chipmunk was trained on technical mailing lists, so most of its labels describe content such as code patches, log output and tables. Our analysis keeps only authored text, so block 10 merges the labels into one authored zone and four zones for text the sender did not write. It adds a sixth zone, markup, matched by regular expressions. We keep the four non-authored zones separate to see how many of each category’s tags come from signatures, banners, quoted messages and other text. [21] To check Chipmunk across the whole corpus, block 10 compares Chipmunk’s zones with zones assigned by regular expressions. The regular expressions mark reply and forward headers, external-sender banners, closing lines and markup. They place the signature after the last closing line and treat lines repeated across many emails as template text. The two methods agree on 73.5% of the 62,906 non-blank lines, and each catches text the other misses. Chipmunk finds signatures in emails with no closing line, confidentiality disclaimers, and attachment and dial-in lines. The regular expressions find external-sender banners, reply headers that carry no “>” marks, and markup. Block 10 therefore combines the two.
[22] Block 10 refines Chipmunk’s zones in two stages. Chipmunk sometimes gives a line a label that clashes with the text around it, and five rules first correct these errors.

Greetings and closings are authored. Greetings and closings (“Dear Dr. Smith”, “Kind regards”) are part of how these emails do their work. Chipmunk’s salutation and closing labels already map to the authored zone. A closing such as “Kind regards,” that Chipmunk labels signature or other also becomes authored.
Disclaimers are banner. Text that Chipmunk labels authored, signature or other but that contains disclaimer wording, such as “intended recipient” or “received this message in error”, becomes banner.
Organization names and job titles inside a signature block are signature. Chipmunk sometimes labels an organization name or job title as authored when the text above and below it is signature. Such text becomes signature unless it ends a sentence.
Sentences inside the message are authored. Chipmunk sometimes labels a sentence as banner or other when the text above and below it is authored. Such a sentence becomes authored if it has four or more words and no tabs.
Signature lines after the message are signature. Chipmunk sometimes labels a whole signature as authored when no closing precedes it. Short lines without sentence punctuation at the end of the message become signature when a signature line follows them or when they hold a name with credentials, a title, an organization or contact details. A sign-off name alone, such as “Sam”, stays authored.

[23] Rule 5 and the attachment and meeting-invitation lines come from the zone check (Section 4.3).
[24] Zones matched by regular expressions then take precedence, in this order: markup, attachment and meeting-invitation lines (other), banner, and quoted, which covers everything from the first reply or forward header on. A line of underscores counts as a reply header only when a “From:” or “De :” line follows it, so meeting invitations stay out of the quoted zone. The banner expressions cover English and French external-sender warnings, disclaimer headings, remote-work notices and land acknowledgements.
